title: The Machine That Predicted the Sky
chapterTitle: A lump of bronze from the sea
look: ARCHIVE bronze, sea and archive stills, slow push

scenes.narration: In nineteen oh one, a boat of sponge divers sheltered from a storm beside a small Greek island and found a wreck forty-five metres down.
They raised marble statues, bronze figures, glassware, and one shapeless lump of corroded metal that nobody thought worth a second look.
The lump went to a museum storeroom in Athens. A year later it split open, and someone saw a gear wheel cut by a Greek hand.
It was a machine the size of a shoebox, made of bronze in the second century before Christ.
At least thirty gears, cut by hand, meshed to carry one motion into another, with a crank on the side to drive them.
On the front, a ring of the zodiac turned behind pointers for the sun and the moon, with a small silvered ball for the moon's phase.
Around it ran a calendar of three hundred and sixty-five days, the Egyptian year, which drifts by one day every four years.
The back carried spiral dials. One counted nineteen years, two hundred and thirty-five months, and folded the calendar back on itself.
Another counted two hundred and twenty-three months: the Saros cycle, which tells when the sun and moon will fall into line and an eclipse is due.
A third dial named the years of the Olympic games. The sky above, and the calendar of a Greek city, on the same piece of bronze.
Its plates were covered in inscriptions: not a dedication, but a manual. Which star rises, what the pointer means, what each dial predicts.
In nineteen seventy-one, Derek de Solla Price read inside it with gamma rays. In two thousand and five, a CT scanner counted the teeth and read the text.
Michael Wright built working models by hand, brass turning on brass, and showed that the machine does what its inscriptions claim.
No gearing of comparable complexity is known from the ancient world, and nothing like it appears again in Europe for more than a thousand years.
So the machine is a fragment of a tradition that was lost: workshops that could cut precision gears, and a client who wanted the sky in his hand.
The ship was a freighter carrying goods west, perhaps Greek art for a Roman villa, and it went down on the way.
It sank with a cargo of luxuries for a Roman buyer, and it was the only thing aboard that could think about the future.
Divers still work those waters, and the wreck has not finished giving up what it carried.
What the workshop was, and who paid for it, still has no answer.
